Cistercian
sis-TUR-shun
adj., n. (of the reforming monastic order founded at Cîteaux in 1098; a monk of that order)
From Latin Cistercium, the Latin name of Cîteaux in Burgundy.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Cistercians were the reform party of western monasticism. In 1098 Robert of Molesme led twenty-one monks out of a comfortable Benedictine house into the marsh at Cîteaux, meaning to keep the Rule of Benedict literally rather than loosely, and above all to restore manual labour to men who had handed it to servants. They wore undyed wool, which is why Europe called them the white monks; they refused the tithes and manors that had made Cluny rich; they settled in waste places and drained, cleared and farmed them. Within Bernard of Clairvaux's lifetime the one house had become some three hundred and forty. This dictionary records them for what they recovered and for what no discipline could reach. They recovered labour, and Scripture dignifies it, “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10), and “In all labour there is profit” (Pro 14:23). They recovered plain worship against ornament. What they could not reach is the standing before God the order existed to secure, because that standing is not won by rule at all, “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28), and “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9). A reform of monasticism was still a reform inside a system that had put a ladder where God had put a gift.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a Cistercian as a monk of the order of Cisteaux, a reformed branch of the Benedictines; an order as a religious fraternity under one rule; reform as amendment of what is corrupt; labour as bodily exertion for subsistence; and austerity as severity of life.

expand to see more

CISTERCIAN, n. A monk of the order of Cisteaux, a reformed branch of the Benedictines, so called from the place of their origin in Burgundy.

ORDER, n. A religious fraternity or society of men, bound by certain rules and living under one discipline.

REFORM, n. A reformation; amendment of what is defective, vicious, corrupt or depraved.

LABOR, n. Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; particularly, the exertion of the limbs in occupations by which subsistence is obtained.

AUSTERITY, n. Severity of manners or life; rigor; strictness; harsh discipline.

Key Scripture

2Th 3:10 — "For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat."

Pro 14:23 — "In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury."

Rom 3:28 — "Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law."

Eph 2:9 — "Not of works, lest any man should boast."

Modern Corruption

The reforming order of Cîteaux, 1098: labour and plain worship recovered, but justification still sought by rule rather than received by faith.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The modern misuse is sentimental rather than ideological: the white monks are made into a lifestyle brand, admired for simplicity and silence by readers who want the aesthetic without the obedience. The Cistercians themselves would have refused the compliment. They went into the marsh to work, and Scripture commends exactly that, “to work with your own hands, as we commanded you” (1Th 4:11).

The real correction runs the other way, and it is doctrinal. A reform that tightens a rule cannot mend what is wrong with rule-keeping as a ground of acceptance. Paul puts the whole weight elsewhere, “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Tit 3:5), and the measure of our best obedience is given plainly, “all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags” (Isa 64:6). The principle to recover is that austerity may discipline a body and can never clothe a soul.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ergazomai (G2038), to labour; Hebrew 'etseb (H6089), toil; Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify; Greek kauchaomai (G2744), to boast; Greek cheir (G5495), the hand.

expand to see more

Greek ergazomai (G2038) — to labour, to work for one's bread; “if any would not work, neither should he eat”, 2 Thessalonians 3:10.

Hebrew 'etseb (H6089) — toil, painful labour, and its profit; “In all labour there is profit”, Proverbs 14:23.

Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, to justify; “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law”, Romans 3:28.

Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to boast, to glory in oneself; “Not of works, lest any man should boast”, Ephesians 2:9.

Greek cheir (G5495) — the hand, as the instrument of honest work; “to work with your own hands”, 1 Thessalonians 4:11.

Usage

"“if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10) — the clause that sent the white monks into the fields."

"“justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28) — what no reform of a rule can supply."

"“all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags” (Isa 64:6) — the measure that humbles the strictest order."
